description: Text formats decomposed: CSV, JSON, YAML, TOML, XML. Their actual semantics, quoting + escaping rules, type systems, common pitfalls, and modern variants (JSONL, JSON5, JSONLD, YAML 1.1 vs 1.2, etc.).

sub_mechanisms.name: CSV_quoting
sub_mechanisms.definition: Field containing comma, quote, or newline must be quoted. Internal quotes doubled. RFC 4180.
sub_mechanisms.why: Embed delimiters safely. Different tools differ on edge cases (Excel uses comma sometimes, semicolon in EU locales). Most-debated text format spec — many incompatible 'CSV' dialects exist.

sub_mechanisms.name: CSV_header_optional
sub_mechanisms.definition: First row may or may not contain column names. No way to tell from data alone — context required.
sub_mechanisms.why: Source of many parsing bugs. Some tools assume header; others assume data. Sniffer heuristics (csv.Sniffer in Python) try to detect. Best practice: always have header.

sub_mechanisms.name: CSV_type_inference
sub_mechanisms.definition: All values are strings. Reader infers types: '1' → int, '1.0' → float, 'true' → bool, '' → null/empty.
sub_mechanisms.why: Type inference is brittle: '01' (zip code) becomes int, dropping leading zero. Dates parsed differently per locale. Best practice: explicit schema or schema-on-read with strict types.

sub_mechanisms.name: JSON_data_model
sub_mechanisms.definition: Object (key-value), array, string, number, boolean, null. No date, no binary, no integer/float distinction.
sub_mechanisms.why: Simple + universal. Number type ambiguity (1.0 vs 1) is JSON's biggest data-quality issue. Lossy round-trip for large integers (JavaScript's 53-bit float limit).

sub_mechanisms.name: JSON_parsing_streaming
sub_mechanisms.definition: Standard JSON requires whole document for valid parse. Streaming parsers (SAX-style) emit events as they go.
sub_mechanisms.why: Large JSON documents (gigabytes) can't fit in memory. Streaming parsers (jq, ijson) emit events; consumer assembles. Trade memory for added complexity.

sub_mechanisms.name: JSONL_NDJSON_streaming
sub_mechanisms.definition: JSON Lines: one JSON value per line. Streaming-friendly by construction.
sub_mechanisms.why: Each line parsed independently. Append-only friendly (log lines). Standard for log files, streaming pipelines, ML training datasets. The 'fixed' JSON for big-data context.

sub_mechanisms.name: JSON_schema
sub_mechanisms.definition: Standard for describing JSON structure (RFC 8927). $schema URL, type, properties, required, format keywords.
sub_mechanisms.why: Validation + documentation. OpenAPI / Swagger uses for API specs. Helps catch mismatches early. Without it, JSON is structurally untyped.

sub_mechanisms.name: YAML_indentation_significance
sub_mechanisms.definition: YAML uses indentation (like Python) to denote nesting. Tabs disallowed by most parsers.
sub_mechanisms.why: Human-readable structure. Whitespace bugs: mixing tabs + spaces, inconsistent indentation. Single source of YAML reliability issues in production (Kubernetes manifests).

sub_mechanisms.name: YAML_norway_problem
sub_mechanisms.definition: Norway's country code 'NO' parses as boolean false in YAML 1.1. Same for 'YES', 'ON', 'OFF'.
sub_mechanisms.why: YAML 1.1's eager boolean parsing. Fixed in YAML 1.2 (only true/false/yes/no, lowercase). Many parsers still default to 1.1. Type-confused values in data is the issue.

sub_mechanisms.name: YAML_anchors_aliases
sub_mechanisms.definition: &name = anchor; *name = alias to it. << = merge key for object inheritance.
sub_mechanisms.why: DRY in config: reuse definitions. Powerful but easy to abuse. Some implementations don't support them; tools differ. Best practice: limit use.

sub_mechanisms.name: TOML_syntax
sub_mechanisms.definition: Sections with [name], key = value. Strict types (string, integer, float, bool, date, array, table). Multiline strings via triple-quote.
sub_mechanisms.why: INI-like clarity + JSON-like typing. Rust's Cargo.toml, Python's pyproject.toml. Less ambiguous than YAML; more readable than JSON for config. Won modern config format wars.

sub_mechanisms.name: XML_attributes_vs_elements
sub_mechanisms.definition: XML: <elem attr='value'>content</elem>. Same data expressible as <elem><attr>value</attr></elem>. Design choice.
sub_mechanisms.why: Persistent debate: attributes for metadata, elements for content; or always elements; or always attributes. Schema (XSD) constrains. Modern XML usage diminishing in favor of JSON.

sub_mechanisms.name: XML_namespaces
sub_mechanisms.definition: Prefix:localName for disambiguation. xmlns:soap='...' declares namespace mapping.
sub_mechanisms.why: Mix XML schemas from different sources. SOAP uses heavily. Parsers must handle namespace resolution. Important historically; less so in modern microservice JSON world.

derivation_rules.name: CSV_universal_but_lossy_typing
then: type information must be conveyed out-of-band
derivation_rules.why: CSV has no types — everything is text. Receiver parses based on assumed schema. Numeric strings, dates, NULLs all ambiguous. Production systems use Parquet / JSON / Avro to avoid this.

derivation_rules.name: JSONL_streaming_friendly
then: it can be processed line-by-line without loading all at once
derivation_rules.why: Each line is independent JSON value. Process millions of lines with constant memory. JSON (single document) requires whole-file load. The streaming choice for big-data JSON.

derivation_rules.name: YAML_complexity_causes_bugs
if: YAML is used for configuration with many edge cases
derivation_rules.why: Indentation, boolean coercion, anchors, multiple specs (1.1 vs 1.2). Same YAML parses differently in different tools. Best practice: minimal YAML, use schemas, prefer TOML/JSON for new config.

derivation_rules.name: JSON_number_precision_loss
derivation_rules.why: JavaScript numbers are 64-bit float. Integers up to 2^53 representable exactly; beyond that, rounded. JSON spec allows arbitrary precision but practical parsers don't. Work-around: large integers as strings.

derivation_rules.name: TOML_for_config_won_over_YAML
if: a new tool needs configuration format
then: TOML is increasingly the chosen default
derivation_rules.why: Rust ecosystem (Cargo) standardised on TOML. Python (pyproject.toml). Many new tools follow. Reasons: less ambiguous than YAML, more readable than JSON, type-rich. The 2020s config trend.
